objectives: Describe the components of a eukaryotic genome.
Explain how chromatin organization regulates the genome.
Classify mutations and reason about mutational signatures.

slides.title: Genome composition: only ~2% codes for protein
slides.body:
**Human genome**: ~3.2 × 10⁹ bp haploid, ~20000 protein-coding genes. The 'gene-centric' picture from Mendel is misleading — protein-coding sequence is the *minority*.

**Coding sequence (~1-2%)**:
- ~20000 protein-coding genes (Human Genome Project ~25000 estimate revised down).
- Exons total ~1% of genome.
- Average gene ~27 kb spanning, ~1300 bp protein-coding (median).

**Introns (~25-30%)**:
- Between exons of coding genes; transcribed but spliced out.
- Median intron ~1500 bp; some massive (DMD has 79 exons + introns >200 kb, total gene 2.4 Mb).
- Contain regulatory elements, alternative-splicing cues, miRNA host sites.

**Regulatory regions (~5-10%)**:
- Promoters: -1 to ~-500 bp upstream of TSS (TATA, Initiator, BRE, DPE motifs).
- **Enhancers**: distal regulatory elements; can act over 100 kb+; bound by tissue-specific TFs; brought into 3D contact via chromatin looping (CTCF, cohesin).
- **Silencers, insulators** (CTCF-bound).
- **3D regulatory architecture**: TADs (topologically associating domains, Dixon + Ren 2012), loops (Rao + Aiden 2014), compartments A/B.
- **CpG islands**: ~30000 in human genome; usually unmethylated, near gene promoters.

**Repetitive elements (~50-55% of genome)** — the *dark matter*:
- **LINEs** (Long INterspersed Elements; ~17%): L1 most active; ~6 kb full length; encode reverse transcriptase + endonuclease for retrotransposition.
- **SINEs** (Short INterspersed Elements; ~13%): Alu (~300 bp; ~1.1 million copies in human) most abundant; use L1 machinery.
- **LTR retrotransposons** (~8%): endogenous retroviruses (ERVs); ~8% of genome — more than coding!
- **DNA transposons** (~3%): mostly fossils in humans; active in plants + flies.
- **Satellite DNA**: tandem repeats. **Microsatellites** (1-6 bp repeats; STRs; CODIS forensics); **minisatellites** (10-100 bp); **centromeric** α-satellite (171 bp repeat in primates); **telomeric** TTAGGG.

**Barbara McClintock** (1902-1992): discovered **transposable elements** in maize 1940s-50s — *jumping genes*. **Ds** + **Ac** elements cause chromosome breaks + variegated kernel color. Largely dismissed for decades — too radical (stable inheritance dogma). **Nobel Prize Physiology/Medicine 1983**, alone, at age 81 — among the most belated recognitions in science. McClintock's transposons rediscovered + generalized: now known active in all kingdoms; foundational for bacterial antibiotic resistance, V(D)J recombination machinery (RAG genes evolved from transposase), HIV integration, modern gene-therapy vectors (Sleeping Beauty, piggyBac), CRISPR delivery, immune evolution.

**Pseudogenes, lncRNAs, miRNAs, snoRNAs**: ~20000 non-coding RNA genes; ~15000 pseudogenes. ~80% of genome is biochemically active (transcribed, bound by TFs, marked) per **ENCODE** consortium (Birney et al. 2012). Function of most non-coding regions still debated.

slides.title: Chromatin, histones, and epigenetic marks
slides.body:
Genome is not naked DNA — it's packaged into **chromatin**. 2 meters of DNA must fit in a 10 μm nucleus → ~7000-fold compaction.

**Nucleosome** (Kornberg 1974; Olins + Olins): 147 bp DNA wrapped 1.7 turns around a **histone octamer** (2 × each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4). H1 linker histone binds linker DNA between nucleosomes.

**Hierarchical compaction**:
- 10 nm 'beads on a string' (nucleosomes).
- 30 nm fiber (debated; solenoid or zigzag).
- Loops + TADs (10⁵-10⁶ bp).
- Chromosomes (10⁷-10⁸ bp).
- A/B compartments (megabase-scale active/inactive territories).

**Histone modifications** (the *histone code*):
- **H3K4me1, H3K4me3** — active promoters/enhancers.
- **H3K27ac** — active enhancers.
- **H3K9me3, H3K27me3** — heterochromatin/repression (Polycomb).
- **H3K36me3** — gene body, active transcription.
- **Writers** (HMTs, HATs), **readers** (bromodomain, chromodomain), **erasers** (HDACs, demethylases).
- **Allis + Jenuwein** histone code hypothesis 2000; Allis posthumous mentions.

**DNA methylation**:
- 5-methylcytosine (5mC) at **CpG dinucleotides** in mammals.
- ~70-80% of CpGs methylated genome-wide.
- **CpG islands** (~30000, 500-2000 bp, GC-rich): typically *unmethylated* near gene promoters; methylation → silencing.
- **DNMTs** (writers): DNMT1 maintenance; DNMT3A/B de novo.
- **TET** enzymes (erasers): oxidize 5mC → 5hmC → demethylation.
- Methylation patterns reset in early embryo (epigenetic reprogramming).
- **Imprinting**: parent-of-origin methylation → monoallelic expression (IGF2/H19, SNRPN/Prader-Willi-Angelman).
- **X-inactivation**: random one-X silenced in females; mediated by XIST lncRNA + heterochromatin marks.

**Chromatin accessibility**:
- **DNase-seq, ATAC-seq, MNase-seq** — open chromatin.
- **ChIP-seq** — TF + histone-mark locations.
- **Hi-C, Micro-C** — 3D chromatin contacts; TADs, loops.
- **CUT&RUN, CUT&Tag** — modern low-input alternatives.

**ENCODE** (Encyclopedia of DNA Elements, NHGRI 2003-2012+): mapped ~80% of human genome as biochemically active. Modulating papers in *Nature* September 2012 issue. Generated reference functional annotations: cell-type-specific enhancers, TF binding sites, accessible chromatin, RNA expression. Roadmap Epigenomics complemented for tissues; 4D Nucleome for 3D dynamics.

**Epigenetic disease + inheritance**:
- ICF, Rett (MECP2), Rubinstein-Taybi (CBP), CHARGE (CHD7).
- Cancer: aberrant DNA methylation; mutant chromatin modifiers (EZH2, DOT1L, KMT2A/MLL fusions in leukemia).
- Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance: documented in plants + worms; controversial but plausible in mammals (Dutch Hunger Winter cohort, holocaust survivor offspring).

slides.title: Mutation types, repeat expansion, and signatures
slides.body:
**Mutations**: heritable changes in DNA sequence. Range from single base to whole-chromosome rearrangements.

**Point mutations / substitutions**:
- **Transitions** (purine ↔ purine, pyrimidine ↔ pyrimidine; A↔G, C↔T): more common.
- **Transversions** (purine ↔ pyrimidine).
- **Synonymous** (silent): doesn't change protein.
- **Missense**: changes amino acid (e.g., Glu6Val in HBB → sickle cell).
- **Nonsense**: introduces stop codon → truncated/degraded protein (NMD).
- **Splice-site mutations**: disrupt splicing → exon skipping, intron retention.
- **Regulatory**: alter expression without changing protein.

**Insertions + deletions (indels)**:
- Small indels: 1-50 bp.
- **Frameshifts** when length not divisible by 3 → typically nonsense/truncation.
- In-frame indels: add/remove aa(s).
- **Stop-loss**: removes stop → readthrough.

**Structural variants (SVs)**: >50 bp.
- **CNVs** (copy-number variants): deletions, duplications. Pediatric disease (e.g., 22q11.2 deletion → DiGeorge), schizophrenia risk, autism.
- **Inversions**: hemophilia A (intron 22 inv of F8 gene).
- **Translocations**: BCR-ABL (Philadelphia chr, CML), MYC-IGH (Burkitt's), EWS-FLI1 (Ewing's).
- **Complex rearrangements**: chromoanagenesis (chromothripsis, chromoplexy) — many breaks + rejoinings in a single catastrophic event.

**Aneuploidy**: chromosome-count changes.
- Trisomy 21 (Down), 18 (Edwards), 13 (Patau).
- Sex-chromosome: XXY (Klinefelter), XO (Turner), XYY, XXX.
- ~5% of all conceptions; most aneuploidies embryonically lethal except for the above + viable trisomies.

**Repeat expansion disorders**:
- **Huntington's disease**: CAG triplet repeat in *HTT* exon 1. Normal <36; affected ≥40. Encodes polyglutamine tract → toxic gain-of-function. Anticipation: paternal transmission expands more (sperm slippage).
- **Fragile X syndrome**: CGG repeat in *FMR1* 5'UTR. Normal <55; premutation 55-200; full mutation >200 → methylation + silencing of FMR1.
- **Myotonic dystrophy** (DM1: CTG in *DMPK* 3'UTR; DM2: CCTG in *CNBP*).
- **Spinocerebellar ataxias** (multiple CAG/other repeat expansions).
- **ALS/FTD**: *C9ORF72* GGGGCC hexanucleotide expansion (most common genetic cause).
- **Friedreich's ataxia**: GAA in *FXN* intron.
- Mechanisms: polyQ aggregation, RNA gain-of-function (foci sequester splicing factors), repeat-associated non-AUG translation (RAN), epigenetic silencing.
- Anticipation: repeats expand each generation → earlier onset, worse phenotype.

**De novo mutations**: ~70 per generation in humans (Kong + Stefansson 2012); ~1.2 × 10⁻⁸ per bp per generation. Paternal age → ~2 extra mutations per year of father's age (sperm replicate more).

**Mutational signatures**:
- **Alexandrov + Stratton 2013-2020**: analyzed >20000 cancer genomes → identified ~80 single-base-substitution signatures (SBS). Each represents a process:
  - SBS1: spontaneous deamination of 5mC at CpG (aging clock).
  - SBS4: tobacco smoking — G→T transversions.
  - SBS7a/b: UV — pyrimidine dimers → C→T.
  - SBS3: BRCA1/2 deficient (HR failure).
  - SBS6/15/20/26: mismatch-repair deficient (Lynch).
  - SBS13/2: APOBEC.
- **COSMIC database** catalogs signatures.
- Indel signatures (ID1-18), DBS, copy number signatures.
- Clinical use: signature → likely cause → targeted therapy (e.g., POLE-mutant → high TMB → immunotherapy responsive; HRD → PARPi).

**Germline vs somatic**:
- Germline mutations: inherited; in every cell of offspring.
- Somatic mutations: accumulate during life; cancer + aging.
- ~3 mutations per gamete per generation; ~10² mutations per somatic cell at birth → ~10⁵ in old age.

question.question: Classify a mutation and predict its consequence
question.goal: A patient's *CFTR* gene has a 3-bp deletion at codon 508 (loss of phenylalanine, ΔF508). Classify + predict consequence.

steps.prompt: What type of mutation is this?

acceptedAnswers: in-frame 3-bp deletion; missense/indel; deletes one amino acid

steps.reveal: 3-bp deletion is *in-frame* (3/3 = 1 codon removed). One amino acid (Phe at position 508) deleted; rest of protein in frame. Not a frameshift, not nonsense, not synonymous — an in-frame indel.

acceptedAnswers: misfolded CFTR; ER-retained; degraded; no chloride channel at apical membrane

hints: CFTR is a chloride channel + Phe508 in NBD1.
steps.reveal: ΔF508 disrupts folding of nucleotide-binding domain 1 (NBD1) → misfolded CFTR retained in ER → ubiquitinated + degraded by proteasome → no functional chloride channel at apical epithelial membrane. Disease: cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive; ~70% of CF alleles in northern Europeans). Phenotype: thick mucus → chronic lung infection, pancreatic insufficiency, infertility.

steps.prompt: How does ΔF508 illustrate the difference between *protein-coding mutation* and *splice-site mutation*?

acceptedAnswers: ΔF508 is coding deletion; splice-site mutations alter splicing motifs

steps.reveal: ΔF508 = coding-region deletion → altered protein sequence (folding defect). Splice-site mutations affect 5'-GU or 3'-AG of introns or branch points → mis-spliced mRNA (exon skipping, intron retention, cryptic splice sites). Different molecular outcomes; different therapeutic strategies. Other *CFTR* mutations include G542X (nonsense → premature stop → NMD) + 1717-1G>A (splice site).

steps.prompt: How do modern CF correctors (e.g., Trikafta) address ΔF508?

acceptedAnswers: small molecules stabilize folding + restore trafficking

steps.reveal: **Trikafta** (elexacaftor + tezacaftor + ivacaftor, Vertex, FDA 2019): two **correctors** (elexa-, teza-) bind misfolded ΔF508 CFTR + stabilize folding → escape from ER → reach apical membrane. **Potentiator** (ivacaftor) increases channel open probability. Treats ~90% of CF patients. Game-changer for CF — life expectancy + lung function dramatically improved. Models precision medicine: variant-specific small-molecule rescue. Earlier: Kalydeco (ivacaftor alone) for G551D gating mutation (~5% patients), then Orkambi, Symdeko, now Trikafta.

question.question: A whole-genome sequence of a melanoma shows >200000 single-base substitutions, dominated by C→T transitions at pyrimidine dinucleotides. Best interpretation?
options: **UV-induced mutational signature** (SBS7a/b in COSMIC catalog). UV radiation causes pyrimidine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, CPDs + 6-4 photoproducts), which when erroneously repaired produce characteristic **C→T transitions at TpC, CpC, and TpT pyrimidine dinucleotides**. Discovery + cataloging: Alexandrov, Stratton 2013-2020 analyzed >20000 cancer genomes → ~80 mutational signatures. Melanoma classically dominated by SBS7. Clinical implications: very high tumor mutation burden (TMB) → many neoantigens → strong response to checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1/PD-L1 blockade, e.g., pembrolizumab, nivolumab). Other signatures: SBS4 = smoking; SBS1 = aging (5mC deamination); SBS3 = BRCA1/2 deficient (HRD).
question.explanation: C→T at pyrimidine dinucleotides = classic UV signature (SBS7 in COSMIC). UV → pyrimidine dimers → C→T transitions. Alexandrov, Stratton 2013-2020 catalogued ~80 mutational signatures from >20000 cancer genomes. Melanoma typically high TMB → strong response to checkpoint inhibitors. Other signatures: SBS1 (aging, 5mC deamination at CpG), SBS4 (smoking, G→T transversions), SBS3 (BRCA-deficient HRD), SBS6/15 (MMR-deficient). COSMIC database catalogs.

hints: What environmental exposure causes pyrimidine dimers?
slides.workedSolution: C→T at pyrimidine dinucleotides = UV signature SBS7 (Alexandrov + Stratton 2013-2020 COSMIC catalog). UV → pyrimidine dimers → C→T transitions. Melanoma classic. High TMB → neoantigens → checkpoint inhibitor responsive. Other signatures: SBS1 aging, SBS4 smoking, SBS3 BRCA-deficient.

question.question: A father carries 38 CAG repeats in *HTT* (just below Huntington's threshold of 40, called intermediate). His daughter has 51 CAG repeats and presents symptoms at age 30. Most likely explanation?
options: **Repeat expansion via anticipation** — particularly with *paternal* transmission. The *HTT* CAG tract is unstable in the male germline (sperm-cell DNA polymerase slippage during repeat replication is biased toward expansion). The 38-repeat intermediate allele expanded across one generation to 51, crossing the disease threshold. Anticipation = earlier onset + worse phenotype with successive generations, characteristic of repeat-expansion disorders. *HTT* CAG expansion → polyQ tract → toxic gain-of-function aggregation in striatal neurons → chorea, cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms. Paternal lineage of expansion much more pronounced than maternal. Other anticipation disorders: fragile X (CGG, maternal expansion bias), myotonic dystrophy (CTG), spinocerebellar ataxias.
question.explanation: CAG repeat expansion via anticipation — paternal *HTT* alleles in intermediate range (27-39) are unstable and prone to germline expansion across the 40 threshold. Daughter inherited expanded allele (51 repeats) → polyQ tract in huntingtin → toxic aggregation in striatal neurons → Huntington's disease at age 30. Anticipation also occurs in fragile X (CGG, often maternal), myotonic dystrophy (CTG/CCTG), SCAs (CAG), C9ORF72 (GGGGCC) ALS/FTD, Friedreich's (GAA). Mechanism: polymerase slippage during germline DNA replication.

hints: What is unstable about the 38-repeat allele?
slides.workedSolution: Paternal *HTT* intermediate alleles (27-39 CAG) expand across generations due to germline polymerase slippage; 38 → 51 crosses 40-threshold for Huntington's. Anticipation = earlier onset + worse phenotype across generations. Mechanism: polyQ tract aggregation in striatal neurons. Repeat-expansion disorders class: HD (CAG, paternal expansion bias), fragile X (CGG, maternal), DM1/2 (CTG/CCTG), SCAs, C9ORF72.

question.question: Human genome ~3.2 × 10⁹ bp, ~20000 protein-coding genes, ~1% exonic. Average coding sequence length per gene (bp)?
question.hint: 0.01 × 3.2e9 / 20000 = 1600 bp coding per gene on average.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how the genome is much more than its protein-coding genes, and what consequences this has for understanding disease.
question.rubric: Mentions: only ~1-2% of human genome is protein-coding; ~25-30% introns; ~50-55% repetitive (LINEs 17%, SINEs 13%, LTR/ERV 8%, DNA transposons 3%, satellites); ~5-10% regulatory (promoters, enhancers, CTCF sites, TAD boundaries); ~10000 lncRNAs + ~2000 miRNAs + tRNAs/snoRNAs/snRNAs. Barbara McClintock (Nobel 1983) discovered transposable elements in maize 1940s-50s — initially dismissed. ENCODE 2012: ~80% biochemically active. Chromatin: nucleosomes + histone modifications (H3K4me3, H3K27me3, H3K27ac, H3K9me3) + DNA methylation (CpG islands) + 3D folding (TADs, loops) → context-dependent gene regulation. Consequences for disease: most GWAS hits are *non-coding* (regulatory variants altering enhancer activity / TF binding / 3D contacts); CNVs/SVs in non-coding regions cause syndromes (22q11.2 → DiGeorge); repeat expansions in UTRs/introns drive Huntington's, fragile X, myotonic dystrophy, C9ORF72 ALS/FTD; mutational signatures (Alexandrov, COSMIC) reveal etiologies of cancer (UV → SBS7 melanoma, smoking → SBS4 lung). The coding-centric view is profoundly incomplete; modern genetics is whole-genome + epigenome-aware.
